headline: Bunker stack thickens off Matinecock as Sound holds early-June slot pattern
subhead: With the Dr. Fish oceanographic feed offline, the read shifts to bait position and tide geometry, and both still favor the western rockpiles on the drop.
body_markdown:
The oceanographic desk is running dark this morning. The Dr. Fish analyst package came across without live buoy values, no Execution Rocks or Kings Point SST figure, and the satellite SST catalog last refreshed on June 4. That leaves the Western Sound report leaning on the previous package's thermal trajectory and on what the water itself has been telling anyone who has run a sounder from Throgs Neck to Lloyd Neck this past week. The pattern is consistent with where early June normally puts us — surface temperatures in the low-to-mid 60s through the main basin, a degree or two warmer inside Little Neck and Manhasset where the shallow flats are charging up on each flood, and a still-cool slug of denser water hanging in the deep slot between Hart Island and Stepping Stones. Wind has been workable, the sea state inside the 40-foot curve is fishable on most stages of tide, and there is no indication of a freshet event or stratification breakdown to scramble the bite.

What that means for this beat is simple. The thermal gradient between the warming bays and the cooler main-stem Sound is the engine right now, and it is pushing adult bunker schools up against the north-shore points exactly where they belong in the first week of June. Matinecock Point, the stretch off Bar Beach, and the rockpile north of Execution are the three pieces of structure to rotate through. Bass in the 28- to 36-inch slot class are the dominant year class, with a sprinkling of legitimate overs mixed in on the bigger bunker pods. The tide that matters is the back half of the outgoing — once the ebb starts ripping off Execution and the bait gets pinned against the south side of the light, that is your window. Stepping Stones on the last of the flood into the early drop is the other piece worth burning fuel on, particularly at first light.

On-the-ground intelligence out of the zone has been consistent for two weeks now. Mojos and bunker spoons trolled along the 30- to 45-foot edges have been the workhorse program, and the size distribution has not changed — heavy on slots, a handful of overs, almost no shorts, which tells you the resident fish are gone and these are migratory bodies still moving through. The bait picture has finally caught up to the predators. There were enough peanut-sized baitfish marking inside the bays through mid-May to keep schoolies honest, but the adult bunker have now stacked along the north shore in the numbers you want to see, and that has shifted the better fish out of the bays and onto the open structure.

Fluke remains a grind on this side. The Oyster Bay to Lloyd Neck drift has been producing mostly shorts with the occasional 17- to 19-inch fish, and drifts have been soft when the wind lays down. The fluke bite west of Eatons Neck typically does not get serious until water pushes past 62 in the deeper sand, and we are not quite there in the channels yet. Porgies are showing on the hard bottom between Hart Island and Execution for anyone willing to anchor up with clam, and that fishery will only improve through the next ten days.

The look-ahead. We are coming off the June 1 new moon, so tides are easing off peak range but still carrying enough water to keep the rips at Execution and the Stepping Stones lit up on the drop. No major frontal passage is staged to disrupt the pattern in the next three to five days, which means the bunker pods should hold their position along Matinecock and continue to draw bass to the same pieces of structure. The variable to watch is surface temperature crossing into the mid-60s in the main basin — once Execution Rocks reads 64 to 65, expect the bigger bunker spoons trolled deep on wire to start outproducing surface presentations, and expect the first legitimate bluefish push to arrive on the back of that warm-up. Until then, the program is the program.

I would be on the water before sunrise, set up west of Execution for the last two hours of the ebb, and have a plug rod rigged for blitzing fish in case a pod of bunker gets shoved against the rocks at the turn. That is where this week is being won.
